description: Somos uma equipe formada por alunos do curso de Análise e Desenvolvimento de Sistemas (ADS) da Fatec Sorocaba, participantes do NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026
summary:
Earth Information Jukebox turns NASA data into sound. Built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, it compares monthly temperatures between two places on Earth using real NASA POWER data. It also lets you "listen" to images of Earth.

It was designed first for blind and low-vision people, so no information depends on sight alone:

Data you can hear: each month becomes a note, and warmer months sound higher. Each region has its own timbre and stereo side. Missing data is silence.
Explained before it plays: a description is read before every sound. Every chart comes with a text summary and a data table.
Screen reader and keyboard: a dedicated Screen Reader First guide and full keyboard navigation.
Low vision: high-contrast mode, visible focus and a 12px minimum text size that scales with browser font settings.
Honest narration: image narration describes only what is actually measured (brightness, contrast, color and position).
It scores 100/100 for accessibility in Lighthouse and 9.2–10 in AccessMonitor (WCAG 2.1). Climate science you can hear.
details:
Earth Information Jukebox is a web app that lets people explore NASA Earth data by ear. It has two experiences:

  • Region comparison: the user picks two places, such as Manaus and London, and a time period. By default this is the last 20 complete years. The app fetches real monthly air temperature (T2M, MERRA-2 reanalysis) from the NASA POWER API. It shows the result in four ways:
    Each region has its own timbre and side of the stereo field, and a month with no data is silent. The chart, table and timeline highlight the month that is currently playing. A map shows the matching NASA GIBS temperature layer for visual context.
    • an audio piece, where each month becomes one note per region and warmer months sound higher;
    • a chart;
    • a written summary;
    • a data table.
  • Listen to an image: users can play a collection of Earth images, including their own. Each image is read in 96 slices. Brightness becomes pitch, contrast becomes intensity, color family becomes instrument and horizontal position becomes stereo placement. A spoken narration describes each image before its sound plays.

What benefits does it have?

Climate data usually reaches people through charts and maps, which leaves blind and low-vision people out. This app is designed screen-reader-first:

  • Every sound is described before it plays.
  • Every chart has a text summary and a data table.
  • Everything works with a keyboard.
  • There is a dedicated Screen Reader First guide and a high-contrast mode.
  • No text is smaller than 12px, and text scales with browser font settings.

Sighted users benefit too, because hearing a trend adds a second way to understand the same data. The app scores 100/100 for accessibility in Lighthouse and 9.2–10 out of 10 in AccessMonitor (WCAG 2.1).

What is the intended impact?

We want to make NASA climate data accessible to people who cannot see it, and show that accessible data visualization can be built in from the start instead of added later. Comparing a familiar place with another part of the world helps people relate global climate data to their own lives.

What tools did we use?

  • Language and framework: TypeScript with React 19, built with Vite, styled with Tailwind CSS.
  • Libraries: React Router, Zustand (state), Recharts (charts), MapLibre GL (map) and Tone.js (audio synthesis).
  • Browser APIs: Web Speech API for narration.
  • Data: NASA POWER Monthly API, NASA GIBS (WMTS tiles and colormaps), plus curated links to the Earth Information Center and the NASA SVS Hometown Dashboard. The base map comes from OpenStreetMap.
  • Hosting and testing: hosted on Vercel; tested with Lighthouse and AccessMonitor.
  • Hardware: none. It runs in any modern browser with no backend.

How is the project creative?

The app treats sound as a real way to read data, not as decoration:

  • Comparable sound: the pitch scale is shared by both regions and evenly spaced in octaves, so the same temperature always produces the same note and equal temperature differences sound like equal intervals.
  • Background music kept apart: for images, an optional background music layer sets the mood. It is clearly separated from the data layer and never carries information.
  • Translated narration: narration reads the text from the page itself, so if the browser translates the page, the voice speaks the translated language.

What factors did the team consider?

  • Scientific honesty:
    • The app uses only real NASA data, never synthetic or silent fallback values. If NASA does not respond, the user sees the error and can try again.
    • Values come from the nearest model grid cell, not the exact city.
    • The app refuses comparisons that would mislead, such as two regions in the same grid cell.
    • If the device cannot draw the map (no WebGL2), the map becomes text.
    • If the browser has no speech voice, narration is disabled with an explanation and the rest of the app keeps working.
  • User control: separate play, pause, stop, speed and volume controls. Audio never starts on its own.
